The biggest tradeoffs are scale and growth, housing costs, and climate. Austin is by far the largest city, Denver is the most expensive and has the coolest, driest climate, while Raleigh is smaller, growing fastest, and generally more affordable.

Austin’s 2025 population is about 1.00 million, compared with 740,613 in Denver and 506,306 in Raleigh. Raleigh had the fastest growth since 2020, at 8.6%, versus 4.2% for Austin and 3.2% for Denver. That points to different growth profiles: Austin offers the largest city population, while Raleigh has expanded more quickly in percentage terms.

Housing is least costly in Raleigh by the supplied measures: median rent is $1,572 and median home value $415,800, compared with $1,729 and $555,300 in Austin and $1,831 and $616,000 in Denver. Denver and Austin report higher median household incomes—$94,718 and $93,658—than Raleigh’s $85,395, but their housing costs are also higher. Raleigh also has the highest owner share, at 50.7%, while Austin has the largest renter share, at 56.6%.

The climate differences are pronounced in the 1991–2020 NOAA normals. Austin has the warmest year overall, with normal highs near 97–98°F in July and August. Raleigh has milder summers, with highs around 89–91°F, but more precipitation in many months. Denver has the coolest winters—January’s normal mean is 32.1°F—and the lowest precipitation throughout the year among the three; the supplied climate data do not provide snowfall values for any of the cities.

Employment and education are relatively similar, though Austin has the highest bachelor’s-degree share at 59.6%, followed by Denver at 56.5% and Raleigh at 54.0%. Raleigh has the lowest 2024 unemployment rate at 4.4%, compared with Austin’s 4.7% and Denver’s 4.9%. Commute times are also close, ranging from 23.0 minutes in Raleigh to 24.9 in Denver. Austin has the highest work-from-home share, at 30.7%, while Denver has the highest transit and walking shares among the three.

For the 2024 FBI city-level figures, Denver has the highest reported violent- and property-crime rates: 993 and 4,761.6 per 100,000 residents. Austin and Raleigh have similar violent-crime rates—466.9 and 488.8—but Raleigh’s reported property-crime rate is lower, at 2,819.2 versus Austin’s 3,241.9. These are city-level reported rates for the same year and should not be treated as a complete measure of overall safety.

Overall, Austin combines the largest population, warmest climate, highest educational attainment, and a large renter and remote-work population, but with higher housing costs than Raleigh. Raleigh offers faster recent growth, lower housing costs, and the lowest unemployment rate, with cooler and wetter conditions. Denver pairs relatively high incomes and somewhat greater transit and walking shares with the highest housing costs, coolest climate, and highest reported crime rates in this comparison.
